The '''1676 Ayuman Cup''', recognised retrospectively as the 5th edition of the '''[[FLLA World Cup]]''', was an international [[Arraby]] tournament contested by the senior men's national teams of the leading Ayuman football associations. It was held in [[Praesyu]], across [[Ayuma]], from 5 June to 2 July 1676, and was won by [[Eldjo]], who defeated [[Emara]] 3–0 in the [[#Final|final]] at the Brimasha Stadium to claim the [[FLLA World Cup#The Andah Cup|Andah Cup]].<ref name="heritage-overview">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1676/overview|title=The 1676 Ayuman Cup: tournament overview|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 June 1763}}</ref>

The competition was staged under the older title of the Ayuman Cup, the name it bore before the [[FLLA]] was constituted and the contest was relaunched and renamed the [[FLLA World Cup]] at the [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700 edition]]; the seven continental confederations did not yet exist, and the field was drawn overwhelmingly from [[Ayuma]], although the competition had by now begun to admit associations from beyond the continent, [[Taval]] of [[Mahea]] appearing among the entrants for the first time. The 1676 finals were organised by a congress of the Ayuman national associations, the informal body that arranged the early editions of the competition.<ref name="heritage-rename">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/history/early-competition-names|title=From the Ayuman Cup to the FLLA World Cup: the early names of the competition|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=12 February 1764}}</ref>

The 1676 edition was contested for the original rotating '''[[FLLA World Cup#The Andah Cup|Andah Cup]]''', the trophy that had been awarded since its introduction at the [[1668 FLLA World Cup|1668 edition]] and that passed to the champion of each tournament. The cup was presented to the victorious Eldjo side at the close of the final. No bespoke permanent trophy was commissioned in 1676; the permanent-trophy tradition that came to characterise the competition began only at the [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700 edition]], after the original cup was lost during the [[Red War]].<ref name="heritage-trophy">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/trophies/the-andah-cup|title=The original Andah Cup, 1656 to 1688|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=2 July 1764}}</ref>

==Host selection==

The 1676 tournament was awarded to [[Praesyu]] by a congress of the Ayuman national associations, the informal body that organised the competition before the foundation of the [[FLLA]]. The Praesyan organisers undertook to stage the finals across five cities, with the principal matches held in the largest city, [[Brimasha]]. The hosting was the first occasion on which Praesyu had staged the competition, and the congress favoured its well-established grounds and central position within [[Ayuma]].<ref name="heritage-host">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1676/host|title=1676 Ayuman Cup: the award of hosting rights to Praesyu|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 June 1763}}</ref>

==Format==

The 12 entered teams were divided into three groups of four for the group stage. Each group operated on a single round-robin basis, with each team playing the other three sides in its group; two points were awarded for a win and one for a draw, in line with the scoring system then in use. The top two teams in each group advanced to the [[#Knockout stage|knockout stage]], together with the two best third-placed teams across the three groups, making up an eight-team knockout. Where teams finished level on points, places were determined first by goal difference and then by goals scored.

The knockout stage consisted of single-elimination ties played over 90 minutes. A tie level at the end of normal time was extended by a single 30-minute period of [[wikipedia:Extra time|extra time]]; under the regulations of the period, any tie still level after extra time was to be settled by a replay rather than by a [[wikipedia:Penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]], a procedure not yet in use. No replay proved necessary in 1676. The two losing semi-finalists contested a [[#Third place playoff|third-place playoff]] on the day before the final.

==Participating teams==
[[File:1676 Ayuman Cup qualification.png|thumb|upright=1.5|{{legend|#000cff|Countries qualified for Ayuman Cup}} {{legend|#ffb400|Country did not qualify}} {{legend|black|Countries that did not enter the Ayuman Cup or were expelled from the tournament prior to playing a match}} {{legend|#ababab|Country outside Ayuma}}]]

Twelve teams took part in the 1676 finals, the majority of them Ayuman national associations. The continental confederations that later structured the [[FLLA World Cup]] had not yet been established, and qualification was settled under the informal arrangements of the period; as host nation, [[Praesyu]] took part automatically. [[Taval]], a [[Mahea]]n association, took part for the first time, an early instance of the competition admitting a side from beyond [[Ayuma]]. The participating teams were:<ref name="heritage-teams">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1676/teams|title=1676 Ayuman Cup: participating teams|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=20 June 1763}}</ref>

==Venues==

Five stadiums in five host cities, all in [[Praesyu]], were used in the final tournament. The principal venue was the Brimasha Stadium in [[Brimasha]], which staged the opening match and the final and was the only ground with a capacity above 22,000. The two semi-finals were divided between the Brimasha Stadium and the Zaraqon Arena in [[Zaraqon]], with the [[#Third place playoff|third-place playoff]] held at Meveran Park in [[Meveran]]. The remaining group-stage fixtures were shared between these grounds and the smaller venues at [[Lorkan]] and [[Drashir]].<ref name="heritage-venues">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1676/venues|title=Host stadiums of the 1676 Ayuman Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=20 June 1763}}</ref>

==Squads==

Each participating association registered a squad of eighteen players, two of whom were required to be goalkeepers; the smaller squads of the period reflected the limited substitution rules then in force, under which a single replacement was permitted only for an injured goalkeeper. A total of 216 players were registered for the tournament.<ref name="heritage-squads">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1676/squads|title=1676 Ayuman Cup: registered squads|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=20 June 1763}}</ref>

==Match officials==

The organising congress appointed a panel of referees and linesmen drawn from the associations not represented in the latter stages of the competition. The opening match was refereed by Halvor Dask of [[Darewa]], and the final by Pell Yaxen of [[Yaxuto]], the senior official of the tournament. The small officiating pool of the period meant that several referees took charge of fixtures involving teams from neighbouring associations, though never from their own.<ref name="heritage-officials">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1676/officials|title=Match officials of the 1676 Ayuman Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=20 June 1763}}</ref>

==Group stage==

The three groups were each contested as a single round-robin. The top two teams in each group advanced to the knockout stage, together with the two best third-placed sides; points were awarded on the two-points-for-a-win system in use at the time, with goal difference and then goals scored used to separate teams level on points.

All dates are given in the local time of the host cities.

==Knockout stage==

The knockout stage involved the eight teams that advanced from the group stage: the three group winners, the three runners-up and the two best third-placed sides. Ties level after 90 minutes were to be extended by a single period of [[wikipedia:Extra time|extra time]]; no tie in 1676 required extra time or a replay.

===Final===

The final was held at the Brimasha Stadium on 2 July 1676 before an estimated crowd of 22,000. [[Eldjo]] took the lead early through Davor Klent, the tournament's leading scorer, and a goal from Tomaz Reska shortly after the interval put the side two clear before Klent added a third in the second half to seal a 3–0 win. [[Emara]], who had reached the final without conceding in the knockout rounds until the closing stages, were unable to find a reply. The victory secured the Andah Cup for Eldjo, which was presented to the Eldjo captain at the close of the match.<ref name="heritage-final">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1676/final|title=The 1676 Ayuman Cup final: Eldjo 3–0 Emara|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 June 1763}}</ref>

==Statistics==

===Goalscorers===

A total of 65 goals were scored in 26 matches, an average of 2.50 per match. The leading scorer was the Eldjo forward Davor Klent, who scored six goals across the tournament, including two in the final. No formal individual awards were presented at the 1676 edition: the leading-player, top-scorer and best-goalkeeper prizes (the [[FLLA World Cup#Awards|Vairan Ball, Marskval and Bastion]]) were not instituted until the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]], and the figures below are recognised retrospectively in the [[FLLA]]'s heritage records.<ref name="heritage-stats">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1676/statistics|title=1676 Ayuman Cup statistical record|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=20 June 1763}}</ref>

==Trophy and significance==

The 1676 edition was contested for the original rotating [[FLLA World Cup#The Andah Cup|Andah Cup]], the same trophy that had been awarded at every edition since its introduction at the [[1668 FLLA World Cup|1668 tournament]]. Under the custom of the period the cup passed to each new champion in turn, and Eldjo's victory placed it in their keeping until the following edition.<ref name="heritage-trophy" />

Eldjo's win came at the expense of the host nation only indirectly: [[Praesyu]] reached the semi-finals and took third place on home soil, while the title was settled between the two Group C qualifiers, Eldjo and [[Emara]], who had been kept apart in the draw until the final. The result was among the more decisive finals of the early editions, Eldjo becoming the first side to win the deciding match without conceding.<ref name="heritage-overview" />

The competition continued under the Ayuman Cup name through the editions of [[1680 FLLA World Cup|1680]] and [[1684 FLLA World Cup|1684]] before the original cup was lost during the [[Red War]] and the contest was relaunched and renamed the [[FLLA World Cup]] at the [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700 edition]].<ref name="heritage-rename" />
